prompt: With the replica cut off from the network, the primary set `stock:MN-330` to 0. What did `GET stock:MN-330` on the replica answer?

choices.text: An error, because the replica knows it lost its primary
choices.why: It knows (`master_link_status:down`) and answers anyway, because `replica-serve-stale-data` is `yes`.

choices.text: The old value, 1
choices.why: Right. A stale read, with no sign in the answer that it is stale.

choices.text: The new value, 0, fetched from the primary on demand
choices.why: A replica never forwards a read; and it could not reach the primary anyway.

choices.text: Nothing, because the key was removed when the link went down
choices.why: The replica keeps its data; it only stops receiving changes.

prompt: Which setting decides whether a Redis replica that has lost its primary answers reads at all?

choices.text: `replica-read-only`
choices.why: That one refuses writes on the replica, not stale reads.

choices.text: `replica-serve-stale-data`
choices.why: Right. Set to `no`, the replica answers most commands with an error while the link is down.

choices.text: `replica-ignore-maxmemory`
choices.why: That one is about memory limits on a replica, lesson 14's territory.

choices.text: `appendonly`
choices.why: That is persistence, lesson 13.

prompt: After `docker network connect`, the replica answered 0 a few seconds later. What does that show?

choices.text: That the replica was consistent all along
choices.why: It answered 1 while the link was down; it was not.

choices.text: That copies agree again once they reconnect
choices.why: Right. Eventual consistency promises the agreement, not when.

choices.text: That the primary resent only the last write
choices.why: How it resynchronised is lesson 15; the point here is the outcome.

choices.text: That reads from a replica are always safe after a reconnect
choices.why: The next partition opens the same window again.

prompt: Ana saves a new address and the reloaded page shows the old one. Which anomaly is it?

choices.text: Lost update
choices.why: Nothing was overwritten; the new address is on the primary.

choices.text: Read your writes
choices.why: Right: her read reached a copy her write had not reached yet.

choices.text: Monotonic reads
choices.why: That needs two reads going backwards; here one read missed her own write.

choices.text: A network partition between the copies
choices.why: No network failed; ordinary replication lag is enough.

prompt: Match each anomaly to what a user sees.
hint: One sight belongs to none of them.

pairs.right: I saved it and the page still shows the old value
the order said shipped, then said paid again
two sales, and the stock went down by one

right_distractors: the page fails with an error

prompt: A team runs MongoDB on a single server with no replicas, so they say the anomalies of this lesson cannot happen to them. Which one still can?

choices.text: None, since there is only one copy
choices.why: One copy does not stop two clients reading, deciding and writing back.

choices.text: Read your writes
choices.why: With one copy every read sees the last write.

choices.text: Monotonic reads
choices.why: There is no second copy to be further behind.

choices.text: Lost update
choices.why: Right. It needs concurrency, not replicas.

prompt: What is the simplest fix for read-your-writes?

choices.text: Read from the primary after that user writes
choices.why: Right. Everyone else may keep reading from replicas.

choices.text: Turn replication off
choices.why: That throws away what the replicas were for.

choices.text: Retry the read until the value changes
choices.why: The client cannot tell an old value from a value nobody changed.

choices.text: Cache the page in the browser
choices.why: A cache serves an old copy; it is a source of the anomaly, not a fix.

prompt: The retry of the payment with `_id: "pay-1001-a7f3"` failed with `E11000 duplicate key error`. How should the application treat that?

choices.text: As a failure to charge, and try again with a new id
choices.why: A new id would make the retry a second payment.

choices.text: As a sign the database is corrupt
choices.why: The unique `_id` did exactly its job.

choices.text: As "already done": the first attempt had landed
choices.why: Right. Here the duplicate-key error is the success case.

choices.text: As a reason to delete the first payment
choices.why: The first payment is the real one.

prompt: The second `updateOne` with `version: 1` answered `matchedCount: 0`. What must the application do next?

choices.text: Nothing: the update succeeded quietly
choices.why: Nothing was changed; ignoring the zero is the lost update again.

choices.text: Read again and decide afresh
choices.why: Right: here it finds the monitor sold out.

choices.text: Send the same update without the version in the filter
choices.why: That sells the monitor twice, the exact bug being prevented.

choices.text: Wait for replication and send it again unchanged
choices.why: Version 1 is gone for good; the same filter will never match.

prompt: Put a write with optimistic concurrency in order.
items: Read the document and note its version
Decide the new value in the application
Update with the old version in the filter, incrementing it
Check matchedCount, and start again if it is 0

prompt: Detecting a conflict at write time with a version number, instead of locking at read time, is called ___ concurrency.
How does Cassandra decide between two writes to the same cell?

choices.text: The write that reached the node last wins
choices.why: Arrival order does not decide; the 179.00 arrived last and lost.

choices.text: The cell with the higher timestamp wins
choices.why: Right, whatever clock produced the timestamp.

choices.text: The coordinator asks the client which one to keep
choices.why: There is no conversation; the rule needs no coordination.

choices.text: It refuses the second write with a conflict error
choices.why: Both were accepted without a word.

prompt: An update was sent with `USING TIMESTAMP 1789000000000000`, older than the cell's. What did the client see, and what was stored?

choices.text: An error, and nothing changed
choices.why: No error came back; that is what makes it dangerous.

choices.text: Success, and the new price 179.00
choices.why: The `SELECT` afterwards still showed 189.00.

choices.text: A warning, and both prices kept
choices.why: A cell holds one value; the older one is discarded.

choices.text: Success, and 189.00 kept
choices.why: Right: the write lost silently.

prompt: One application server's clock runs a minute ahead. What happens to the products it updates?

choices.text: Its writes lose to everybody else's for a minute
choices.why: That is a clock that is behind.

choices.text: Nothing, since Cassandra uses the node's clock
choices.why: Drivers assign timestamps from the client's clock, as cqlsh did here.

choices.text: Others' corrections in that minute lose to its writes
choices.why: Right, as the 199.00 lost to the future-stamped 159.00.

choices.text: Cassandra rejects timestamps from the future
choices.why: It accepted one from late 2027.

prompt: A node's clock is 2 seconds behind. By how many microseconds are its write timestamps too low?
For which data is last-write-wins a safe rule? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A customer's last-seen time
choices.why: Right: a newer value simply replaces an older one.

choices.text: A stock count two checkouts decrement
choices.why: Read-modify-write on a shared cell is the lost update, with the clock choosing the loser.

choices.text: A profile field only its owner edits
choices.why: Right: one writer, nothing computed from the old value.

choices.text: An account balance
choices.why: Every change depends on the value before it.

prompt: A support agent says: "the customer changed their phone number, it showed the old one, and a minute later the new one". Which anomaly is it, and which fix fits?

choices.text: Lost update; add a version number
choices.why: Nothing was lost: the new number appeared a minute later.

choices.text: Read your writes; read from the primary
choices.why: Right. The write landed; the read came from a copy behind it.

choices.text: Clock skew; synchronise the clocks with NTP
choices.why: Skew makes a value lose for good, not appear late.

choices.text: A partition; wait for the network
choices.why: Ordinary replication lag produces this without any failure.

prompt: Which of these needs no replica at all to go wrong?

choices.text: A page that reads its own write from a secondary
choices.why: That needs a secondary behind the primary.

choices.text: Two checkouts reading stock 1 and both writing 0
choices.why: Right: the lost update needs only concurrency.

choices.text: A replica answering with the old value after a disconnect
choices.why: That is a replica, by definition.

choices.text: Two reads from two replicas going back in time
choices.why: Two replicas, by definition.

prompt: Right after `docker network disconnect`, the replica's `INFO` still said `master_link_status:up`. Why?

choices.text: Because the disconnect had not taken effect yet
choices.why: It had: the replica already missed the write of 0.

choices.text: The replica notices silence only after `repl-timeout`
choices.why: Right. Silence is not an error until the timeout says so.

choices.text: Because `INFO` is answered by the primary
choices.why: The command ran on the replica, which could not reach the primary.

choices.text: Because Docker keeps the old connection open
choices.why: The connection is gone; the replica simply has not heard nothing for long enough.

prompt: A customer refreshes an order page twice: first it says "shipped", then "paid". Which anomaly is it?

choices.text: Monotonic reads
choices.why: Right: two reads hit replicas behind by different amounts. Each answer is legitimate; the sequence goes backwards.

choices.text: Lost update
choices.why: Nothing was overwritten; the status is "shipped" on the primary.

choices.text: Read your writes
choices.why: The customer did not write anything.

choices.text: Clock skew
choices.why: No timestamps decided anything here.

prompt: A payment service lets MongoDB generate an `ObjectId` for each insert, and retries on timeout. What goes wrong?

choices.text: Nothing: the retry fails with a duplicate-key error
choices.why: Each attempt gets a fresh id, so nothing is duplicated as far as the index knows.

choices.text: A payment that had landed is charged twice
choices.why: Right. The id has to exist before the first attempt.

choices.text: The retry waits until the first insert is visible
choices.why: Nothing links the two attempts.

choices.text: MongoDB rejects inserts after a timeout
choices.why: It accepts both.

prompt: Which defence does the section give against clock skew deciding a stock count?

choices.text: NTP, and no read-modify-write on a shared cell
choices.why: Right: or pay for a lightweight transaction where the write must be conditional.

choices.text: Raise the replication factor so more copies vote
choices.why: More copies change nothing about which timestamp wins.

choices.text: Write every update twice
choices.why: The second write carries the same skewed clock.

choices.text: Read at consistency `ALL` so every replica is asked
choices.why: Every replica holds the same winning cell; the read cannot recover the loser.
